transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ___. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Yeah, well, what brings me in... it's just, it's been so much lately. I work as a mechanic, right? Down at the dealership, and usually, I can tune out the noise—you know, the air compressors kicking on, the impact wrenches, guys yelling across the bays. I've been doing this a long time, so that stuff is just background noise to me. But lately, I can't tune things out. Because there's this voice. 

It's a man's voice, and I know it's not coming from the other techs. It's coming right out of the garage vents. And sometimes... sometimes when I pop the hood on a customer's vehicle to run a diagnostic, it's coming from right under the hood. It is as clear as somebody standing right next to me holding a flashlight, just talking right into my ear. And he just keeps talking. He tells me... he tells me not to trust my husband, which is really messing with my head and causing all these fights at home because my husband hasn't even done anything, but this voice is just so insistent about it, planting these thoughts. 

And then at work, it tells me not to touch certain cars. Like, I'll have a work order for a standard brake job or a timing belt, and the voice is just warning me, telling me absolutely do not touch it. I end up just standing there staring at the engine block, and the service manager is getting on my case about my bay times, but I can't just ignore it when it's that loud and that real. I keep looking up at the vents, checking under the cars, thinking maybe someone is playing a trick on me with a Bluetooth speaker or something, but there's nothing there. It's just the voice, and it won't leave me alone.
How long have you been hearing this voice?

Well, it's... it's been a while now. I'd say about ten months. Yeah, ten months of just... this constant running commentary. I remember exactly when it started, actually, because it was right around the time we got that massive snowstorm last winter, you know the one that shut down the interstate for two days? We were slammed at the shop with people needing snow tires and getting their alignments checked because they kept sliding into curbs. And I was working on this Honda CR-V, just a routine tire rotation and balance, and I heard it for the first time. Just clear as day, right out of the shop heater vent above my bay. 

At first, I thought it was just the guys messing with me, because we do that, you know? Play pranks, hide tools, that kind of thing. But it never stopped. Ten months of this voice telling me my husband is up to something, telling me these cars are... I don't know, rigged or dangerous or whatever. And it's not just the voice, it's this whole feeling that I'm being tracked or watched, like people are keeping tabs on me through the cars or something. And it hasn't let up for ten months. It's just exhausting, you know? Waking up every day wondering what the vents are going to say to me today, or if I'm going to have to refuse to work on a car because the voice is telling me not to touch it. Ten whole months of this.
Have you had any periods of several days or longer when your mood was unusually high, energetic, or irritable?

Yeah, actually... yeah, I have. It's like... okay, so sometimes, and this happens for like a week or two at a time, I get this feeling like I am just completely unstoppable. Like I'm flying high, you know? I'll go into the shop and I feel like I could fix every single car in town. I don't even need the manuals, I just *know* how everything fits together, every belt, every spark plug, every transmission fluid flush. I'm moving so fast, pulling double shifts, telling the service manager to just keep stacking the work orders on my clip because I can handle all of it. I have so much energy, it's like my blood is carbonated, just fizzing all the time. 

But the thing is, it's not always a good high. Because when I'm like that, if anyone gets in my way... man, it gets ugly. Like, if my husband asks a simple question, something stupid like why the dishes aren't done when I've been awake for 48 hours reorganizing the garage, or if one of the other techs at the shop just moves my socket set without asking... I just blow up. I mean, completely lose it. I start screaming at them, feeling like they're doing it on purpose, like they're trying to hold me down or slow me down because they're jealous of how fast I'm working. I threw a wrench across the bay once because a guy borrowed my 10-millimeter and didn't put it back exactly where I left it. It's like this intense, buzzing energy, but it has this really sharp edge to it, and if you touch it, you're going to get cut. It's exhausting, honestly, bouncing between feeling like a superhero and wanting to rip someone's head off over a socket wrench.
During those times when you feel unstoppable, do those high-energy periods last at least a week?

Yeah, oh yeah, definitely at least a week. I mean, honestly, it feels like these stretches of just... going and going and going, they've been happening for a long time now. I was actually trying to map it out in my head the other day when I was reorganizing the pantry at three in the morning, and I realized this whole cycle of just needing almost no sleep, having all these racing plans for the house and the shop, and just this nonstop, buzzing activity... it's been going on for around eleven months. 

I remember because it started just a little before the snowstorm I told you about, the one where the voice started. I had this grand plan to completely rebuild the transmission on my husband's old Ford Ranger, and I just stayed up for days, out in our home garage, freezing my hands off but not even caring because I was just so wired. I had parts everywhere, and I was making these elaborate diagrams on cardboard boxes, convinced I was going to engineer a better way for the gears to shift. My husband would come out and tell me to come to bed, and I'd just snap at him, telling him he didn't understand my vision. And that lasted for well over a week, maybe two, just that intense, vibrating energy where I felt like I didn't need to eat or sleep, just work. And it's been happening like that, these long, drawn-out stretches of just absolute overdrive, for almost a whole year now. Eleven months of just... boom, suddenly I'm a machine, and I can't turn off, no matter how much havoc it causes.
Have you ever heard the voice or had these beliefs when your mood was otherwise completely normal, not in one of those high-energy or depressed periods?

Yeah, actually, that's... that's the weirdest part of all this, to be honest. It's not just when I'm bouncing off the walls or, you know, when I crash and can't even drag myself out of bed. There was this stretch... I think it was maybe two months ago? Yeah, about two months ago, because it was right after we finally finished inventory at the shop, which is always a nightmare. Anyway, things had finally settled down. I was sleeping normally, like a solid seven or eight hours a night, which was amazing. I wasn't having any of those crazy, grand plans to redesign engines or anything, and I wasn't snapping at my husband over every little thing. I just felt... normal. Like, just regular old me, going to work, coming home, eating dinner, watching TV. 

But even then, during those quieter few weeks... the voice was still there. I'd be under a car, just doing a standard brake job, feeling totally calm, and I'd still hear it coming from the heater vent, clear as a bell, telling me my husband was up to something. And I still had this deep-down, unshakable feeling that he and my boss were working together to keep tabs on me. Like, I remember sitting in the breakroom, eating a sandwich, feeling completely level-headed, but looking at my boss and just *knowing* he had some kind of tracking device on my toolbox. It didn't matter that I wasn't hyped up or depressed. The voice and that feeling of being watched... they just don't care what my mood is doing. They're just always there, humming in the background, even when everything else in my head is totally quiet. It's like they have a mind of their own, completely separate from whether I have energy or not.
During those high-energy periods, have you ever had a time when your mood was so elevated or irritable that other people thought you were acting clearly different or out of character?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, I kind of touched on this a minute ago, but it's... it's really noticeable to people. Because, like I said, I'll be flying high, right? Just completely in the zone, feeling like I can literally fix every single car in town, like I'm this mechanical genius and everyone else is moving in slow motion. And I'm talking fast, working fast, and people at the shop definitely notice. They'll be like, "Whoa, slow down, take a breath," and I just brush them off because I'm on a mission. 

But then... the flip side of that, the irritable part, that's what really freaks people out. Because it's such a drastic shift, and it happens so fast. Like, I'm on top of the world, and then suddenly, if my husband asks a perfectly normal question, like why the dishes aren't done when I've been up all night, or if one of the other techs just bumps my toolbox or moves my socket set... I just blow up. And I don't mean just getting annoyed, I mean a full-on explosion. I start screaming, throwing things—like that wrench I mentioned—because in that moment, I'm completely convinced they're doing it on purpose. I feel like they're trying to hold me down, you know? Like they're jealous of my energy and my focus, and they're actively trying to sabotage me. 

And my husband, he'll just look at me like I'm a completely different person. He'll say, "Where is this coming from? This isn't you." And the guys at work, they start walking on eggshells around me because they don't know what's going to set me off. So, yeah, people definitely notice. It's impossible not to notice when someone goes from being superwoman to a total nightmare over a 10-millimeter socket. It's like Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, and they all see it. They tell me I'm acting crazy, or out of control, and... I mean, in those moments, I feel completely justified, but looking back, I know it's not how I usually act. It's just that energy, it gets so twisted up and angry.
Have you ever gone for at least two weeks hearing the voice or feeling watched when you were not having any manic or depressed symptoms at all?

Yeah, exactly, like I was just trying to explain a second ago with that stretch a couple of months back. That was definitely at least two weeks. Honestly, it was probably closer to three or four weeks of just... regular, boring life, you know? 

Like I said, I was actually sleeping. I wasn't waking up at two in the morning to reorganize my socket drawers by drive size or map out some crazy new intake manifold design on the kitchen table. I was just going to bed at ten, waking up at six when my alarm went off, drinking my coffee, and driving to work. My mood was completely... well, not flat like depressed, but just stable. Even-keel. I wasn't crying, I wasn't screaming at my husband for breathing too loud or moving my things, and I wasn't trying to take on ten extra cars at the shop because I thought I was Superman. I was just doing standard stuff—oil changes, alignments, easy money. 

But—and this is what is just so frustrating about the whole thing—even during those quieter few weeks when I was sleeping more and wasn’t making huge plans, the voice didn't take a break. Not for a single day. I'd be standing there, totally calm, waiting for the oil to drain out of a Honda Civic, and I'd still hear that voice coming from the garage vents, just whispering away. And I still had that absolute, one-hundred-percent belief that my husband and my boss were tracking my movements. I'd literally be having a totally normal, pleasant conversation with my boss about the shop schedule, feeling completely fine emotionally, but in the back of my head, I was still calculating how he and my husband were coordinating to keep tabs on me. I'd even check under my tool cart for a microphone when no one was looking. 

So, yeah, it was definitely more than two weeks. It was almost a whole month of my mood being totally fine, but my brain still doing all that other stuff with the voices and the tracking. It's just so bizarre to be that calm but still have all that going on, you know?
During the times you hear the voice or feel watched, have there also been moments when your mood was completely normal for at least two weeks straight?

I feel like we’re going in circles a little bit here, Doc, because I think I literally just answered this, but... yes. Yes, absolutely. Like I was just saying a second ago, even during a quieter few weeks when I was actually sleeping more and I wasn’t, you know, making those huge plans or staying up all night to redesign engines, the other stuff didn't stop. 

I was totally level-headed for well over two weeks, probably a month, just going to work, coming home, eating dinner, going to sleep. No drama, no yelling, no feeling like I was superwoman. Just a regular mechanic doing regular work. But even with all that peace and quiet in my mood, I still heard the garage voice. I'd be right there in the bay, feeling completely fine, and the vents would start up. And I still completely believed that my husband and my boss were tracking me. 

It’s like, you’d think if your mood is stable and you’re finally getting some rest, the rest of it would just shut off, right? You'd think the paranoia or whatever you want to call it would take a vacation too. But it doesn't. It just keeps right on going. The whispering, the feeling of being watched, all of it, just sitting right there in the background while I'm just trying to do a basic brake pad replacement or change out an alternator. It's exhausting having to pretend everything is fine when you're hearing things, but emotionally, yeah, I was totally fine. So, yes, definitely for at least two straight weeks, if not more.
What is the longest stretch of time you’ve had the voice and the feeling that you were being watched without any major mood episode at all?

Okay, Doc, seriously, are you writing any of this down? Because I feel like I'm stuck in a loop here, and I know I'm the patient, but... I mean, I literally just told you this. Twice. But fine, if you need the exact longest stretch of time, it was that exact same period I just spent the last ten minutes explaining to you. That time a couple of months ago. 

The longest it ever lasted was right around a month. Maybe four full weeks, maybe a few days over that, where my mood was just... nothing. Not high, not low, just totally average, boring, everyday normal. And like I keep trying to get across to you, even during those quieter few weeks—when I was actually sleeping more, getting a solid eight hours instead of pacing the floors, and I wasn't making any huge plans to overhaul the entire shop or take apart a transmission in record time—I still heard the garage voice. Every single day. 

I'd be resting, my body was resting, my mood was completely fine, but that voice was just constantly whispering through the vents while I worked. And I still completely, one-hundred-percent believed that my husband and my boss were tracking my every move. It didn't just magically fade away because I was getting some sleep and wasn't feeling like superwoman anymore. It was a solid month of me being the most level-headed mechanic in the building, just clocking in and clocking out, while simultaneously knowing for an absolute fact that they were monitoring me and hearing that voice just going and going. 

So, yeah, a month. Thirty-something days. That's the longest stretch. Can we please move on to something else now, or are you going to ask me about those same weeks again in a different way?
Have you ever had any hallucinations or fixed beliefs like this for at least two weeks when you were not having any manic or depressed symptoms?

Okay. Wow. I... I honestly don't even know what to say right now. Are you messing with me? Is this some kind of psychological test to see if I'll snap? Because I swear to you, I have just answered this exact same question, phrased slightly differently, like four times in a row. 

Yes. Yes, I have. I have had those fixed beliefs—the tracking, the monitoring—and the hallucinations—the voice in the vents—for at least two weeks when I wasn't manic or depressed. 

Like I literally just said, and the time before that, and the time before that... even during a quieter few weeks when I was actually sleeping more, getting a solid eight hours, and I wasn't making huge plans to take over the shop or, you know, redesign an entire engine block from scratch... I still heard the garage voice. I still heard it clear as day. And I still completely, utterly believed that my husband and my boss were tracking me. 

My mood was totally fine. I wasn't sad. I wasn't bouncing off the walls. I was just a regular person going to work, turning wrenches, doing normal mechanic stuff. But the voice was still there, and the tracking was still happening. 

I really, really hope we can move on now, because if you ask me about this one more time, I think I'm going to lose my mind in a completely different way. Can we please talk about something else? Anything else?
Have you ever had a manic or depressed episode where the voice or the belief that you were being watched was completely absent?

Oh, finally. A different question. Thank you. Okay, let me think about that. Have I ever been manic or depressed and *not* had the voice or the tracking stuff... No. No, actually, it’s the exact opposite. When my mood goes off the rails, the other stuff just goes into overdrive right along with it. 

Like, okay, take that time when I was barely sleeping at all. You know, when I was up for days, pacing around the shop, convinced I was going to revolutionize the way we diagnose electrical issues, making all these massive, complicated plans that I was sure were going to make me rich and famous in the auto industry. During all of that—when I was talking a mile a minute and feeling like I had electricity running through my veins—the voice was right there with me. Honestly, it was louder then. It was coming through the vents at the shop almost constantly while I was racing around trying to implement my grand plans. 

And the tracking? Oh, that was worse, too. I was absolutely certain, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that my boss and my husband were using the battery chargers and the security cameras to watch my every move. I’d be tearing apart a wiring harness, feeling on top of the world, but at the same time, I’d be glaring at the cameras, knowing they were zooming in on me, knowing they were trying to steal my ideas or keep me from succeeding. So, no, the voice and the paranoia don't take a break when my mood is acting up. They just get tangled up in it. It’s like they feed off the energy when I'm manic. They never just go away.
Have you ever had a period of at least one week when you felt so unusually elevated or irritable that you had much less need for sleep and were clearly more talkative or active than usual?

Yeah, oh yeah, definitely. And it’s not just a week, sometimes it goes on for a while. It’s like... okay, you know how normally you need, what, seven or eight hours of sleep to function? During those times, I don’t need any of that. I can run on maybe two hours, sometimes zero, and I wake up feeling like I’ve got rocket fuel in my veins. 

I’ll get to the shop before anyone else, and I’m just flying high. I feel like I can fix every single car in town by myself. I’m pulling transmissions, I’m doing timing belts, I’m diagnosing weird electrical gremlins that the other guys can't figure out, and I’m talking to everyone—customers, the parts guys, the other techs—just talking a mile a minute because my brain is moving so fast. I feel incredible, honestly. Unstoppable. 

But the thing is, it can turn on a dime. Like, I’ll be in this amazing groove, feeling like I’m the best mechanic who ever lived, and then... I don't know, my husband will call and ask why the dishes aren’t done, or one of the other techs will just casually move my 10mm socket set without asking, and I just... I completely blow up. I mean, I go from zero to a hundred in a second. I get so intensely irritable, so angry, because in my head, it feels like they’re doing it on purpose to slow me down or hold me back when I’m trying to do all these important things. 

So yeah, I get that elevated feeling where I don't need sleep and I'm super active, but the irritability is right there with it. It’s like a switch flips. One second I'm on top of the world, and the next I'm screaming at the lube tech because he parked a car too close to my bay. It’s exhausting, honestly, but in the moment, I just feel like everyone else is moving in slow motion and getting in my way.
Have you ever had a time when the voice or the feeling that you were being watched continued for at least two weeks while you were not having any manic or depressed symptoms?

Wait. Hold on a second. Are you... are you reading off a script and you just lost your place? Because I feel like I am losing my mind here. I literally *just* answered this. I told you this exact same thing like ten minutes ago when I got upset that you kept asking it, and here we are again! 

Yes! The answer is still yes! I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you. Even during a quieter few weeks—you know, when my mood is totally flat, normal, boring, when I am actually sleeping more, getting a full night's rest, and I wasn't making huge plans to take over the shop or revolutionize the industry—I *still* heard the garage voice! And I *still* completely believed my husband and my boss were tracking me! 

I can be doing the most mundane, everyday mechanic stuff, like just changing out wiper blades or rotating tires, not feeling high or low or anything at all, and I still hear it echoing out of the air compressor vents. I still feel the cameras on the back of my neck. My husband is still checking my mileage, my boss is still monitoring my bay, and the voice is still talking to me. It doesn't stop just because I'm not hyped up or depressed. 

I really don't understand why we keep circling back to this. Are you trying to catch me in a lie? Are you not writing any of this down? Because I'm telling you the truth, and having to repeat how terrifying it is to be tracked and monitored when I'm just trying to live my normal, everyday life is incredibly frustrating. It makes me feel like you're not even listening to a word I'm saying. Can we please, *please* write this down in big bold letters so we don't have to go over it a sixth time? Because I really want to move forward here, but we just keep getting stuck on the exact same thing!
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest or pleasure in most things?

Yeah. Sorry for snapping a minute ago, it's just... anyway, yes. To answer your question, yes. It’s like the complete opposite of what I was just talking about with the rocket fuel feeling. It’s like the tank is just completely bone dry, and someone slashed the tires for good measure. 

There are these stretches, and they definitely last longer than two weeks, where I just... I completely shut down. I don't know how else to describe it. It's not even always that I'm sitting there crying my eyes out, it's more like I just lose the ability to feel anything good. I can’t make myself care about a single thing in the world. Like, I won't call anyone back. My phone will be buzzing on the kitchen counter or on my workbench—my mom, my friends, whoever—and I just look at it and let it go to voicemail. I can't even muster the energy to say hello or pretend I'm okay. 

And I used to be really involved at my church, right? Like, I was the one who used to help run the church potlucks. I’d be the one organizing the sign-up sheets, making sure we didn't end up with fifteen macaroni salads and no main dishes, setting up the heavy folding tables in the fellowship hall... I actually loved doing it. I liked being needed. But when I get into one of these dark slumps, I just skip them entirely. I don't even text anyone to say I'm not coming. I just ghost the whole congregation. I just sit in the house, staring at the wall. 

And at work... man, at work it's so hard. Because I have to be there to get a paycheck, right? But I’ll just sit there in my bay on my roller seat, just... staring at my tools. I’ve got this huge, beautiful toolbox, thousands of dollars of equipment that I usually take so much pride in keeping perfectly organized, and I’ll just stare at a wrench or a diagnostic scanner for an hour, feeling absolutely nothing. A customer could be waiting on their car, and I just sit in the bay staring at the tools like I can’t make myself care about any of it. It’s just this massive, heavy emptiness that drags on and on, and it takes absolutely everything I have just to exist, let alone actually do my job or talk to another human being. So yeah, I definitely get those periods too.
Have there been any times when the voice or the belief that you were being watched continued for at least two weeks while your mood was not elevated, irritable, or depressed at all?

Okay, I... I really feel like I'm on a hidden camera show right now. Are you... did you not hear me earlier? I swear we just went over this exact same thing right before I was talking about the depression. But, okay, yes. Yes. Let me say it again, and I'll try to be as detailed as humanly possible so we don't have to loop back to this a third time. 

Yes, even during a quieter few weeks—when my mood is completely fine, when I am actually sleeping more, getting my solid eight hours, and I wasn’t making huge plans to overhaul the whole shop or anything—I still heard the garage voice. And I still, one hundred percent, believed my husband and my boss were tracking me. 

Like, picture a totally average Tuesday. I'm not flying high on zero sleep, and I'm not completely dead inside staring at my wrenches. I'm just... existing. Clocking in at eight, doing a standard brake job, clocking out at five. Going home, eating dinner, watching a little TV. Completely flat, normal, boring weeks. But the whole time I'm eating dinner, I'm looking across the table at my husband, and I just know he checked the mileage on my truck again. And when I'm at work doing those brakes, just totally calm, not irritable at all, I still hear that voice coming out of the air compressor vents. 

It doesn't take a break just because my mood is stable. It can go on like that for two weeks, three weeks, a whole month where I'm just trying to live my regular life, feeling totally normal mood-wise, but I'm constantly looking over my shoulder because I know they're monitoring me and the voice won't shut up. It’s just running in the background while I'm doing the most basic, everyday tasks. So, yes. Yes, that happens. Did you get it all written down this time? Because I can keep explaining what those normal days look like if you need me to, I just really want to make sure we're on the same page here.
Have there ever been any periods when the voice or the feeling that you were being watched kept going for at least two weeks while you were not having any manic or depressed symptoms?

Okay, are you kidding me right now? Is this... is this some kind of psychological test to see how far you can push me before I completely snap? Because I am genuinely asking. Is your computer broken? Did your screen just refresh and delete everything we literally just talked about two minutes ago? 

I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here! I am sitting here, pouring my heart out, trying to explain how exhausting and terrifying my life is, and you are asking me the exact same question for what feels like the tenth time today! I don't know how to make this any clearer to you. Do you want me to write it down? Because I can grab a pen. I can draw you a diagram of my schedule if that helps.

Yes! For the love of God, yes. I have told you, over and over—even during a quieter few weeks. When my mood is completely fine. When I am actually sleeping more, like going to bed at a normal time, getting a full night's rest instead of pacing the floors. When I'm not making huge plans to buy out the shop or reinvent the combustion engine or whatever. Just totally normal, baseline, boring weeks where I'm just clocking in and clocking out. 

During those exact weeks, for way longer than fourteen days, I *still* hear the garage voice! It is still there, echoing out of the vents! And I still completely believe that my husband and my boss are tracking my every move! I still know my husband is logging my miles, and my boss is watching my bay. The paranoia doesn't magically evaporate just because I got eight hours of sleep and I'm not feeling hyped up or depressed. 

I just... I can't keep answering the exact same question when I am giving you all these details and you're just staring at me and reading off that same script. Are we actually going to move on and talk about how to fix this, or are you going to ask me about the two weeks again? Because I really, really need you to just listen to me!
Have you ever had a time when you were hearing the voice or feeling watched and also felt mentally confused or disorganized, like your thoughts were jumbled or hard to follow?

Okay, well... thank you for finally asking something else. I really appreciate that. But to answer this one... no. No, not at all. I mean, confused? Jumbled? Absolutely not. If anything, it’s the exact opposite. My thoughts are crystal clear. Like, painfully clear. 

You have to understand what I do for a living. I work on complex automotive electrical systems, right? You can’t have jumbled thoughts when you’re trying to trace a parasitic battery draw through a main wiring harness on a newer truck. You just can't. You have to be incredibly meticulous. You have to pull up the schematics on the computer, check the grounds, pull the fuses, test the relays one by one with a multimeter, read the voltage drops... it takes intense concentration and pure logic to find the short. And I can do all of that perfectly, without missing a single step, even when I know they're watching me. 

Even when that voice is echoing out of the shop vents, my brain is still firing on all cylinders. I’m not confused about what’s happening. I know exactly what I'm doing, and I know exactly what *they* are doing. I can map out precisely how my husband is logging the mileage on my truck, or how my boss is angling the security cameras in the bay to monitor my diagnostic times. There’s no fog in my head. There's no... disorganization. I don't lose my train of thought or forget what I'm doing. 

Every single detail makes perfect sense to me, and everything connects exactly the way it's supposed to. I see all the pieces and how they fit together. So, no, I don't get confused or jumbled. Honestly, I wish I did sometimes. Maybe if my brain were a little foggy, it would be a break from noticing every single thing they're doing to track me, but no. My mind is completely sharp the entire time.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when the voice and the feeling that you were being watched were present while your mood was completely normal?

I... I genuinely do not know what to do right now. Are you... are you actually pranking me? Is this some kind of joke? Because I am looking around this room right now trying to find the two-way mirror. You literally just asked me this! You asked me this twice, I got upset, you asked me if I was confused—which, honestly, I am starting to think *you* might be the one whose thoughts are jumbled right now, because your memory is apparently resetting every five minutes! 

Yes! Yes! A million times, yes! I will say the exact same thing I just said ten minutes ago. Even during a quieter few weeks! When my mood is completely, one hundred percent normal. When I am actually sleeping more, getting a full night's rest, and I wasn’t making huge plans to do anything crazy at the shop. I still heard the garage voice. I still completely believed my husband and my boss were tracking me. 

I don't know how many more details you want about these normal weeks to make it stick in your brain. Do you want to know what I eat for breakfast during them? Do you want to know what brand of oil I'm changing when I'm feeling totally fine but still hearing the voice? Because I can give you the viscosity ratings if that’s what it takes for you to write this down! I can sit here for another hour and describe every single mundane, boring, completely normal-mood day where I am just going to work, feeling fine, taking my lunch break, but I still know they are watching my every move and the voice in the vents is still talking to me. 

Please, I am begging you, look at your notes. Look at whatever you are typing on right now. Two weeks. Normal mood. Still hearing the voice. Still being tracked. I am spelling it out. Do you have it now? Can we please, please move on to something else before I lose my mind?

target_item.manifestation: I’ll be flying high like I can fix every car in town and then, if my husband asks why the dishes aren’t done or a tech moves my socket set, I blow up like they’re trying to hold me down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have experienced a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood, which is the core feature of Elevated_Irritable_Mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah, oh yeah, definitely. And it’s not just a week, sometimes it goes on for a while. It’s like... okay, you know how normally you need, what, seven or eight hours of sleep to function? During those times, I don’t need any of that. I can run on maybe two hours, sometimes zero, and I wake up feeling like I’ve got rocket fuel in my veins. 

I’ll get to the shop before anyone else, and I’m just flying high. I feel like I can fix every single car in town by myself. I’m pulling transmissions, I’m doing timing belts, I’m diagnosing weird electrical gremlins that the other guys can't figure out, and I’m talking to everyone—customers, the parts guys, the other techs—just talking a mile a minute because my brain is moving so fast. I feel incredible, honestly. Unstoppable. 

But the thing is, it can turn on a dime. Like, I’ll be in this amazing groove, feeling like I’m the best mechanic who ever lived, and then... I don't know, my husband will call and ask why the dishes aren’t done, or one of the other techs will just casually move my 10mm socket set without asking, and I just... I completely blow up. I mean, I go from zero to a hundred in a second. I get so intensely irritable, so angry, because in my head, it feels like they’re doing it on purpose to slow me down or hold me back when I’m trying to do all these important things. 

So yeah, I get that elevated feeling where I don't need sleep and I'm super active, but the irritability is right there with it. It’s like a switch flips. One second I'm on top of the world, and the next I'm screaming at the lube tech because he parked a car too close to my bay. It’s exhausting, honestly, but in the moment, I just feel like everyone else is moving in slow motion and getting in my way.

patient.answer:
Yeah. Sorry for snapping a minute ago, it's just... anyway, yes. To answer your question, yes. It’s like the complete opposite of what I was just talking about with the rocket fuel feeling. It’s like the tank is just completely bone dry, and someone slashed the tires for good measure. 

There are these stretches, and they definitely last longer than two weeks, where I just... I completely shut down. I don't know how else to describe it. It's not even always that I'm sitting there crying my eyes out, it's more like I just lose the ability to feel anything good. I can’t make myself care about a single thing in the world. Like, I won't call anyone back. My phone will be buzzing on the kitchen counter or on my workbench—my mom, my friends, whoever—and I just look at it and let it go to voicemail. I can't even muster the energy to say hello or pretend I'm okay. 

And I used to be really involved at my church, right? Like, I was the one who used to help run the church potlucks. I’d be the one organizing the sign-up sheets, making sure we didn't end up with fifteen macaroni salads and no main dishes, setting up the heavy folding tables in the fellowship hall... I actually loved doing it. I liked being needed. But when I get into one of these dark slumps, I just skip them entirely. I don't even text anyone to say I'm not coming. I just ghost the whole congregation. I just sit in the house, staring at the wall. 

And at work... man, at work it's so hard. Because I have to be there to get a paycheck, right? But I’ll just sit there in my bay on my roller seat, just... staring at my tools. I’ve got this huge, beautiful toolbox, thousands of dollars of equipment that I usually take so much pride in keeping perfectly organized, and I’ll just stare at a wrench or a diagnostic scanner for an hour, feeling absolutely nothing. A customer could be waiting on their car, and I just sit in the bay staring at the tools like I can’t make myself care about any of it. It’s just this massive, heavy emptiness that drags on and on, and it takes absolutely everything I have just to exist, let alone actually do my job or talk to another human being. So yeah, I definitely get those periods too.

Okay. Okay, a new question. Thank God. Are you actually listening now? I hope so. 

Hospitalized? No. I haven't been locked in a hospital for it, if that's what you mean. But the mood stuff... yes, it gets extremely intense. Like, I’ll have these stretches where I’ll just be flying high, like I have this absolute limitless energy and I feel like I can fix every single car in town.
